title: Loopio vs Wolfia for RFP and DDQ automation
summary: Loopio vs Wolfia for RFPs, DDQs, and security questionnaires: content library versus self-maintaining knowledge base, seats versus work, and portals.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR**


- Loopio is built around a curated content library that a proposal team owns and governs. Wolfia is built around a knowledge base assembled from documents your company already maintains.
- Loopio publishes no dollar amounts. Its pricing page shows three editions, Foundations, Enhanced, and Enterprise, and the entry edition is described as including 10 seats.
- Wolfia has no per-seat or per-viewer fees and includes unlimited users, so adoption spreading past the proposal team does not change the bill.
- The dividing line in practice is who keeps the answers current: a librarian on your team, or the source documents themselves.
- Both are reasonable buys. Which one fits depends on whether your volume is scheduled sales RFPs or unscheduled inbound security review.


## What Loopio is built around


Loopio is a response management platform for RFPs, RFIs, security questionnaires, and DDQs, and its center of gravity is the content library. You store approved answers once, then reuse and govern them across every response, with AI-assisted suggestions, automatic question categorization, SME review workflows, and connectors to sources like SharePoint and Google Drive sitting on top.


That model earned its reputation for a reason. When many contributors touch one response, a governed library is how the company stops sending five different versions of the same answer. Our fuller review of[Loopio reviews, pricing, and alternatives](https://wolfia.com/blog/loopio-reviews-pricing-alternatives) covers the strengths and the friction points teams report, including imports of non-standard documents and export formatting.


The trade-off is ownership. A content library is an asset somebody has to keep current, and that somebody is usually a proposal manager whose calendar already belongs to deadlines.


## What Wolfia is built around


Wolfia starts from the documents that already exist: policies, architecture notes, prior responses, security reviews, and the pages behind your trust center. It indexes them, and re-indexes them when they change, so an answer reflects the current version of a policy because the policy changed rather than because someone remembered to update a library entry.


Every answer carries a citation back to the document it came from. That changes what review means. A reviewer is checking a source rather than reconstructing an argument, which is the difference between a two-minute pass and a twenty-minute one on a question about data retention.


The mechanics of that are in our write-up on[building a questionnaire knowledge base that maintains itself](https://wolfia.com/blog/build-a-questionnaire-knowledge-base-that-maintains-itself) .


## How does Loopio pricing work?


Loopio does not publish dollar amounts. Its[pricing page](https://loopio.com/pricing/) lists three editions, Foundations, Enhanced, and Enterprise, and routes all three to a call for a custom quote tailored to your requirements. The Foundations edition is described as including 10 seats and suited to smaller, sales-led RFP teams.


Seats are the thing to model before you sign. Response work is contributor-heavy by nature: the security lead writes the security section, an engineer answers the architecture question, legal reviews the data processing language, and a sales engineer assembles the whole thing. Each of those people is a seat, and the number of them tends to grow in the same quarter the volume does.


Wolfia is[priced around the work](https://wolfia.com/pricing) instead. There are no per-seat or per-viewer fees, one platform includes unlimited users, and pricing scales with questionnaire and review volume rather than headcount. Pulling in a fifth engineer to answer one question is free, which matters more than it sounds when the alternative is a Slack thread asking someone to paste an answer on your behalf.


## Who keeps the answers current?


This is the question that decides the evaluation, and it is worth asking both vendors directly.


In a content library model, currency is a job. Someone reviews entries on a schedule, retires stale ones, and updates the library when a policy is rewritten or a subprocessor is added. Skip a cycle and the library keeps confidently suggesting last year's answer, and the reviewer has no signal that anything is wrong.


In a source-indexed model, currency is a property. The subprocessor list is answered from the subprocessor page, so updating the page updates the answer. The failure mode moves from stale content to bad source documents, which is a problem you can see and fix.


Neither model removes the human. Both put the human somewhere different.


## RFPs and DDQs are not the same document


An RFP is scheduled, long, and mostly about capability and commercial terms. A DDQ is triggered, structured, and mostly about how your company is run. A security questionnaire is triggered, structured, and mostly about controls and evidence.


A platform built RFP-first handles all three through one library workflow, which works when the language is repetitive procurement prose. It works less well on the questions that are specific to your architecture, because those answers were never in the library to begin with. If you are scoping the DDQ side specifically, our guide to[DDQ automation software](https://wolfia.com/blog/due-diligence-questionnaire-guide-ddq-examples) covers the evaluation criteria, and[RFP meaning in business, plus RFI, RFQ, and DDQ](https://wolfia.com/blog/rfp-meaning-business-guide) sorts out which document is which.


## Portals, spreadsheets, and the return trip


Drafting an answer is half the job. The other half is getting it back into whatever the buyer sent, which is a spreadsheet with merged cells, a Word document with a table per control, or a portal with a login and no export button.


The[Wolfia Chrome extension](https://wolfia.com/products/chrome-extension) fills the portal in place from the same corpus that answers everything else, including portals that never let you export, and handles nested tables, checkboxes inside cells, and conditional questions that only appear after you answer the one above them. Ask any vendor you evaluate for the specific list of portals it fills and what happens on one that has no export.


[See Wolfia answer an RFP and a DDQ from your own documents Book a demo](https://wolfia.com/demo?ref=blog)


## Where Wolfia fits


Wolfia is built for security, GRC, and sales engineering teams whose response volume arrives unscheduled. The parts that come up most in a Loopio comparison:


- **A knowledge base that maintains itself.** Source documents feed it as they change, with no curation cycle to run.
- **A citation on every answer.** Each draft links to the document behind it, so review is verification.
- **Pre-approved answers where wording is fixed.** Legal-approved language ships word for word when it has to.
- **Answer routing to a reviewer.** Sensitive answers reach the right person before they go out.
- **Unlimited users.** Contributors are not a line item, so the people who know the answer can write it themselves.


## Which one should you pick?


Pick Loopio if your volume is scheduled sales RFPs, you have a proposal function that owns content governance, and a curated library is an asset your team already treats as valuable.


Pick Wolfia if your volume is inbound security questionnaires and DDQs, if it lands without warning, and if the answers live in documentation that already exists rather than in a library nobody has had time to build. The tell is simple. Count how many hours last quarter went into maintaining answers rather than writing them. If that number is large, the library is the cost, not the cure.


## Final Thoughts


Loopio and Wolfia both remove the retyping. They disagree about where the truth lives. One keeps it in a library your team curates, the other keeps it in the documents your company already maintains and re-reads them for you. That single choice determines who spends their Fridays keeping answers current, which is the real cost of either system.
